strengths: Introduces a novel and practical formulation of latent-space anonymization for video foundation models, avoiding retraining of frozen encoders and enabling plug-and-play privacy preservation.

Proposes SPLAVU with a lightweight Anonymizing Adapter Module (AAM) and three well-motivated training objectives: clip-level self-supervised privacy preservation, multi-task co-training, and latent consistency.

Extensive evaluation across privacy (VISPR, gait) and multiple utility tasks (action recognition on Kinetics400/UCF101/HMDB51, temporal action detection on THUMOS14, anomaly detection on UCF-Crime) and several backbones (I3D, VideoMAE-B, VJEPA-H, InternVideo-H, VideoMAEv2-G).
Demonstrates substantial privacy leakage reduction (e.g., ~29-35% relative cMAP reduction) while maintaining near-baseline utility, with strong data efficiency and computational efficiency.
Provides thorough ablations on AAM architecture, loss components, task generalization, latent consistency weight, attention heads, and precomputed features.
Introduces new protocols for assessing perceived gender bias in action recognition and shows SPLAVU can reduce subclass accuracy gaps, adding a responsible-AI dimension.
The paper is generally clear, well-structured, and includes a detailed appendix with implementation details and training algorithm.
weaknesses: Privacy evaluation is empirical and limited: it mainly relies on attribute classifiers on VISPR static clips and does not consider adaptive attackers, nonlinear/deep attackers, feature inversion, or formal privacy guarantees. The privacy classifier is inconsistently described as linear in the main text and as a 2-layer MLP in the appendix.

Main utility results train the anonymizer on the same tasks used for evaluation (AR/TAD/AD), so the 'generalization to unseen tasks' claim is supported only by an ablation with non-trivial drops (e.g., TAD mAP 56.45 vs 60.82 when trained only on AR). Some claims of staying 'within 1-2%' are overstated.

The method largely combines existing components (NT-Xent contrastive loss, multi-task co-training, L2 latent consistency) with moderate algorithmic novelty, and lacks direct comparison to other latent/feature-space anonymization or differential-privacy-based baselines.

Privacy evaluation uses VISPR, an image dataset of static attributes, rather than actual video private attributes. Temporal privacy is only partially addressed: with latent consistency, gait recognition remains relatively high (53.45% vs 69.73% baseline), so the 'privacy beyond pixels' claim is not fully realized for motion-based attributes.

Prior input-level anonymization methods are compared mainly using I3D, while large video foundation model experiments only compare against raw features, leaving broader baseline comparisons on modern backbones missing.
The bias protocols are artificial, use a binary gender formulation, and show modest absolute gap reductions; the bias contribution is secondary and may overstate 'first' claims.

Reproducibility could be improved: no explicit code release is mentioned, and sensitivity to all loss weights and training choices is not fully explored, with some details only in the appendix and minor inconsistencies across sections.

strengths: Introduces a latent-space anonymization formulation for video foundation models, avoiding pixel-level retraining and enabling a plug-and-play adapter on frozen encoders.
Comprehensive evaluation suite across action recognition, temporal action detection, and anomaly detection, with several video backbones including I3D, VideoMAE, VJEPA, InternVideo, and VideoMAEv2.
Lightweight Anonymizing Adapter Module with low trainable parameter count and efficient training; demonstrates data efficiency and scalability to large models.
Includes extensive ablations on adapter architecture, loss components, task combinations, data scale, and number of attention heads.
Attempts to address gender bias in action recognition and proposes new bias evaluation protocols, showing reduced subclass accuracy gaps.
Provides implementation details and a training algorithm in the appendix, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Critical mismatch between the privacy threat model and evaluation: privacy is evaluated on static clip representations, but the actual stored/shared features used by downstream utility tasks are temporal clip features. The privacy loss explicitly targets static clips, so the paper does not demonstrate that the temporal features stored for video understanding are anonymized. An attacker using temporal features could likely recover private attributes.

Privacy evaluation uses a relatively weak attacker (linear/MLP on VISPR static clips) and does not consider adaptive, nonlinear, or reconstruction-based attackers. Reported cMAP remains around 50 after anonymization, which may not constitute strong privacy protection.

Inconsistent privacy evaluation details: the main text states a linear classifier is used on static clip representations, while the appendix describes a 2-layer MLP for private attribute prediction; it is unclear which setup produces the main privacy numbers.

Bias mitigation claims are not supported by comparisons to dedicated debiasing baselines (e.g., ALBAR, group DRO) and rely on limited protocols and datasets. The 'first' claim is questionable given cited prior work on bias in action recognition.

The method is not truly task-agnostic: it requires co-training with task-specific heads and labels for seen tasks. Unseen tasks still degrade (e.g., TAD drops by over 4 mAP when not trained on), and latent consistency trades off privacy for utility/gait privacy.

Novelty is incremental: adapter modules, contrastive objectives, consistency losses, and multi-task co-training are standard components. The paper lacks comparisons to simple latent-space obfuscation baselines or other representation anonymization methods.

Several central claims are overstated: the 35% privacy reduction applies mainly to I3D, while large models show about 29%; 'near-baseline utility' hides task-specific drops and requires training on all tasks; 'first generalizable method' is not fully supported by the evidence.

Some technical details are unclear: how the AAM reasons across the temporal dimension when applied per clip, how static clips are constructed and processed by the video encoder, and how maximizing NT-Xent avoids feature collapse. Equation (1) is also malformed.

strengths: Introduces a novel and practical formulation of latent-space anonymization for video foundation models, using a lightweight plug-and-play Anonymizing Adapter Module (AAM) on frozen encoders, avoiding costly retraining of large utility models.

The training framework is well motivated and carefully designed: a clip-level self-supervised privacy objective, a multi-task co-training utility objective, and a latent consistency loss. Ablations convincingly show the importance of each component, especially latent consistency for generalization to unseen tasks.

Evaluation is extensive and strong across five downstream tasks (action recognition on Kinetics400/UCF101/HMDB51, temporal action detection on THUMOS14, anomaly detection on UCF-Crime) and multiple backbones (I3D, VideoMAE-B, VJEPA-H, InternVideo-H, VideoMAEv2-G), demonstrating a favorable privacy-utility tradeoff and data efficiency.

Adds useful secondary contributions: new protocols for assessing perceived gender bias in action recognition (NTU-Bias-F/M and Toyota Smarthome) and evidence that latent anonymization can reduce subclass accuracy gaps, sometimes while improving overall accuracy.
Good reproducibility: detailed implementation, hyperparameters, dataset protocols, training algorithm, and efficiency analyses are provided in the main paper and appendix.
weaknesses: The privacy evaluation relies on a linear attacker on VISPR attributes; stronger/adaptive attackers or reconstruction attacks are not considered. The claim that private information is 'removed' may be stronger than the evidence, since cMAP remains around 50 in several settings.

Comparisons to prior input-level anonymization methods are mainly on I3D. For large foundation models, only raw-feature baselines are reported, which is understandable but leaves the scalability comparison against alternative privacy mechanisms incomplete.

The gender-bias contribution is interesting but not deeply benchmarked against dedicated debiasing methods; it uses a single shortcut action in NTU and limited real-world evaluation, making it feel somewhat orthogonal to the main privacy contribution.

The clip-level privacy objective is largely heuristic: maximizing NT-Xent between static clips from the same video lacks a rigorous theoretical justification for why it selectively suppresses private attributes while preserving utility.

Related work on latent/feature-level privacy and task-agnostic representation obfuscation is relatively thin, and a broader discussion of alternative latent privacy approaches would better position the contribution.

strengths: Introduces a novel formulation of privacy preservation in the latent space of video foundation models, avoiding pixel-level anonymization that requires retraining utility models.

Proposes a lightweight Anonymizing Adapter Module (AAM) that is plug-and-play with frozen video encoders, reducing trainable parameters by up to 88.7% compared to prior methods and enabling fast, data-efficient training.

Employs three well-motivated training objectives: clip-level self-supervised privacy preservation, co-training utility retention, and latent consistency, with ablations validating each component's importance.

Provides extensive evaluation across five downstream tasks (action recognition, temporal action detection, anomaly detection, retrieval, gait recognition), multiple datasets (Kinetics400, UCF101, HMDB51, THUMOS14, UCF-Crime, VISPR, VP-HMDB51/101, Casia-B, NTU, Toyota Smarthome), and multiple backbones (I3D, VideoMAE-B, VJEPA-H, InternVideo-H, VideoMAEv2-G).

Achieves strong empirical results: e.g., 35.5% relative reduction in VISPR cMAP privacy leakage while maintaining utility within 1–2% across action recognition, temporal action detection, and anomaly detection.
Matches a supervised privacy baseline without using private attribute labels, demonstrating the effectiveness of the self-supervised privacy objective.
Demonstrates data efficiency by training on small datasets like HMDB51 and generalizing across tasks, with the latent consistency loss enabling generalization to unseen tasks.
Includes an analysis of attack resistance, showing that black-box inversion fails to recover private attributes, and provides qualitative reconstruction analysis.
Introduces new protocols for assessing gender bias in action recognition and shows that the proposed anonymization reduces subclass accuracy gaps on both synthetic and real-world bias settings.
The paper is clearly written with a thorough appendix covering implementation details, additional ablations, and supplementary experiments.
weaknesses: The method anonymizes only global clip-level embeddings ([CLS]/pooled features), leaving patch-wise tokens unprotected. This limits applicability to dense tasks such as segmentation or captioning and to scenarios where patch tokens are stored or shared; the authors acknowledge this as future work.

Privacy protection is considerably weaker for temporal features used by utility tasks: on VP-HMDB51 and VP-UCF101, cMAP drops only from 76.4 to 70.5 and 75.9 to 69.6 respectively, leaving private attributes still predictable well above random chance. The headline 35% reduction is based on static VISPR evaluation, not on the temporal features actually shared for downstream tasks.

The method is vulnerable to white-box inversion attacks: when the attacker has access to the anonymizer f_A, cMAP recovers to 73.7 on VP-HMDB51 (vs. 76.4 raw), indicating that privacy is not robust if the model is known. The paper dismisses this as unrealistic, but in many deployment scenarios the anonymizer could be public or inferable, and no formal privacy guarantee is provided.

The clip-level privacy objective (maximizing NT-Xent between two static clips from the same video) is heuristic and lacks theoretical grounding. It does not directly minimize mutual information between features and private attributes, and it is unclear why it should remove attributes that are present in each individual frame rather than only shared across frames.

Missing feature-space anonymization baselines (e.g., adding noise, PCA, autoencoder without adversarial privacy loss, or direct mutual information minimization) make it difficult to isolate the benefit of the proposed specific objectives versus any latent-space perturbation.

No error bars or statistical significance tests are reported for the main results. Some utility drops are very small (e.g., 0.1–0.2%) and could be within noise, which weakens the claim of near-baseline utility preservation.

Comparisons to prior input-level anonymization methods are conducted only on I3D, not on modern video foundation models. While this may be due to impracticality of retraining large models, it limits the positioning of the method against existing approaches.

The gender bias contribution is somewhat orthogonal and may overclaim being the first to introduce protocols for gender bias in action recognition, given prior work on bias in action recognition (e.g., ALBAR). The absolute bias reduction is modest, and the method was not designed for debiasing.

The co-training utility objective requires labels for predefined utility tasks; if the target tasks are unknown or not included during anonymization training, utility on unseen tasks drops (e.g., TAD mAP from 60.82 to 56.45 when only action recognition is used). This limits the claim of fully general task-agnostic anonymization.

strengths: Novel formulation of latent-space anonymization for video foundation models, enabling privacy-preserving feature sharing without retraining the utility encoder.
Lightweight Anonymizing Adapter Module (AAM) with well-motivated objectives: clip-level self-supervised privacy loss, multi-task utility co-training, and latent consistency regularization.

Extensive evaluation across multiple downstream tasks (action recognition, temporal action detection, anomaly detection, retrieval, gait) and multiple video backbones (I3D, VideoMAE, V-JEPA, InternVideo, VideoMAEv2-G).

Strong empirical privacy-utility tradeoff in the black-box threat model: large VISPR cMAP reduction while maintaining near-baseline utility, with data efficiency and scalability to large foundation models.
Introduces new gender-bias evaluation protocols for action recognition and demonstrates that latent anonymization reduces subclass accuracy gaps without an explicit bias objective.
Thorough ablation studies on adapter architecture, loss components, task generalization, and attack resistance, plus detailed implementation and training algorithm in the appendix.
Practical efficiency: frozen encoder, precomputable features, and significantly fewer trainable parameters than prior pixel-level anonymization methods.
weaknesses: Privacy is not robust to white-box attacks: Table 8 shows white-box inversion recovers private attribute prediction close to raw features (cMAP 73.7 vs 76.4 on VP-HMDB51), undermining the central privacy claim. The threat model is not sufficiently formalized, and this limitation is not highlighted in the abstract.

The main privacy evaluation uses a weak 2-layer MLP attacker; cMAP can fall below random chance (e.g., 41.07 on VISPR), suggesting the metric may not reliably measure leakage. Stronger or ensemble attackers are needed.

Temporal private attribute privacy is modest: on VP-HMDB51/VP-UCF101, cMAP only drops from ~76 to ~70, and gait recognition remains high with the default latent consistency (53.45 vs baseline 69.73). The claim of mitigating motion-based attributes is conditional and not fully supported.

Missing baselines for large foundation models: for VideoMAE/V-JEPA, only raw features are compared; prior pixel-level methods and simple latent obfuscation baselines are not adapted, limiting the strength of the empirical comparison.
No variance or statistical significance is reported for main results or bias mitigation; small gap reductions (e.g., 9.42 to 5.44) may be within noise, and multiple runs would strengthen the claims.

Some claims are overstated: the headline '35% reduction in privacy leakage' is based on static VISPR attributes, while video-specific temporal attributes show much smaller reductions; 'within 1-2%' utility preservation does not always hold for unseen tasks (e.g., THUMOS14 drops >4 mAP when trained only on AR) or for I3D anomaly detection (2.6% drop).
Bias protocols rely on binary perceived gender labels; details on how gender labels were obtained are lacking, and the ethical implications of gender labeling are not fully discussed.
Some table inconsistencies/confusing experimental setups (e.g., Table 5 vs Table 6) make it difficult to compare results across ablations and may hinder reproducibility.

strengths: Introduces a novel and practical problem formulation: latent-space anonymization for video foundation models, enabling privacy-preserving feature sharing without retraining the frozen video encoder.

The proposed Anonymizing Adapter Module (AAM) is lightweight and plug-and-play, with three well-motivated objectives (clip-level self-supervised privacy, multi-task co-training, latent consistency) that together support multi-task utility and generalization.

Extensive empirical evaluation across five downstream tasks (action recognition, temporal action detection, anomaly detection, retrieval, gait recognition) and multiple backbones (I3D, VideoMAE-B, VJEPA-H, InternVideo-H, VideoMAEv2-G) demonstrates a strong privacy-utility tradeoff, reducing privacy leakage by ~29-35% while maintaining near-baseline utility.

Thorough ablations cover AAM architecture, loss components, seen vs. unseen tasks, training set scale, attack resistance, reconstruction attacks, compute efficiency, and feature precomputation, providing good insight into design choices.
The paper proposes new protocols for evaluating perceived gender bias in action recognition and shows that latent anonymization can reduce subclass accuracy gaps without an explicit bias objective.
Reproducibility is supported by detailed implementation hyperparameters, training algorithm, dataset splits, and compute/parameter analysis.
The work has clear practical relevance for privacy-preserving video understanding and feature storage/sharing in real-world deployment scenarios.
weaknesses: The claimed temporal communication of the AAM is not fully clear: if f_A operates on a single global clip-level embedding, self-attention over a single token reduces to a linear transformation, making the 'communicate across the temporal dimension' claim potentially overstated. The paper should clarify whether AAM processes sequences of clips or each clip independently.

Privacy protection is empirical and heuristic rather than formally guaranteed (e.g., no differential privacy). The method is not robust to white-box inversion attacks, and the threat model for a publicly available anonymizer needs more discussion.

The main evaluation may use seen tasks during anonymization training, while the abstract's claim of preserving utility within 1-2% applies mainly to those seen tasks. Generalization to unseen tasks, especially temporal action detection, shows larger drops (e.g., ~4.4 mAP), so the distinction between seen-task performance and zero-shot generalization should be made clearer.

The bias evaluation lacks comparisons to dedicated bias mitigation baselines (e.g., ALBAR) and relies primarily on subclass accuracy gap as the fairness metric. The binary perceived gender formulation is acknowledged as limited, but the bias protocols could be strengthened with additional fairness metrics and baselines.

Comparisons to prior privacy-preserving methods are mostly limited to the I3D backbone; while prior latent methods for large VFMs do not exist, the paper could better position its results against relevant feature-space or representation-level privacy methods from adjacent areas.

The latent consistency loss weight is critical and the default setting (ω_LC=100) appears to trade off privacy for utility; a more systematic analysis of this tradeoff and guidance for choosing it would strengthen the paper.
